enrichment.short_title: Land registry rectification for disputed axe-head boundary
key_facts: Carmen Johnson and Walter Shaw disputed ownership of an 'axe head' parcel and a side-land right of way at Cornhill Farm near Chester.
The judge held the axe head was excluded from Shaw's 1968 and 1982 conveyances and refused rectification of Johnson's registered title.
The Land Registry had extended Johnson's title after her solicitors showed a drain line and Shaw's solicitors failed to respond to a September 2000 letter.
Shaw had paper title to the axe head, had used the land for farming, and had erected a temporary fence after travellers occupied the garage site.
The Court of Appeal held the axe head was conveyed in 1968, Shaw had long-held paper title, and rectification should be ordered; damages on account were set aside.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against a High Court judge's order favouring the claimant on boundary, right of way, trespass and damages, and dismissing Shaw's counterclaim for rectification.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part: rectification ordered for the axe head; payment on account of damages quashed; right-of-way interference findings not challenged.
enrichment.ratio: Where verbal parcel descriptions in conveyances prevail over 'identification only' plans, acreage differences between the 1920 and 1968 conveyances establish that the axe head passed to Shaw; on rectification under section 82 the court exercises discretion having regard to section 82(3) policy but need not require an overriding interest under section 70(1)(g), and here paper title, long use and the claimant's contribution to the registry error favoured rectification despite her being registered proprietor in possession.
legal_issues: Construction of 1968 and 1982 conveyances as including the axe head
Whether refusal of rectification under section 82 was correct
Relevant date for overriding interest under section 70(1)(g) on administrative registration
Whether a payment on account of damages was supported by evidence

enrichment.short_title: Murder conviction appeals after joint assault on Leonard Proctor
key_facts: Two 16-year-olds were convicted of murdering Leonard Proctor after attacks outside the Miners' Arms, Trimsaran, on Christmas Day 2000.
Jones admitted violence but denied causing fatal injuries; Jenkins denied participation in the second attack.
Mrs Rees heard a youth say he did not care if he went down for murder while Jones was with a girl in the road.
The judge did not direct that Mrs Rees's evidence exculpated Jones and gave no cut-throat co-defendant caution.
Fresh evidence from a custodial officer that Jones had told her Jenkins was innocent was received for Jenkins; both convictions were quashed and retrials ordered.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals to the Court of Appeal with leave against murder convictions and, for Jones, against the section 82A minimum term; fresh evidence heard on Jenkins's appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeals against conviction allowed; retrials directed; appellants remanded in custody pending Crown Court bail applications.
enrichment.ratio: Where Mrs Rees's evidence placed the self-inculpatory 'murder' remark with a youth on the pavement while Jones was in the road, inviting the jury to consider Jones as its maker was a misdirection capable of serious prejudice to a defence denying fatal violence; and where co-defendants give adverse evidence, a judge should normally warn the jury to treat each defendant's evidence with care because of possible self-interest, following Knowlden and Cheema rather than treating Burrows as a general bar on such warnings.
legal_issues: Misdirection on Mrs Rees's exculpatory evidence for Jones
Failure to warn the jury about cut-throat co-defendant evidence
Whether the judge unduly discounted a road-traffic cause of fatal injuries
Admissibility of fresh custodial-officer evidence on Jenkins's appeal under section 23

confidence.notes: Clear unsafe-conviction reasoning on two misdirection grounds plus fresh evidence for Jenkins.

enrichment.short_title: Refusal to conjoin paroxetine non-infringement declarations
key_facts: Apotex sought declarations of non-infringement under section 71 in respect of GSK's GB2297550 paroxetine hydrochloride patent.
Revocation and infringement actions over the same patent were due for an expedited ten-day trial before Pumfrey J.
Apotex wanted declarations that three alternative manufacturing processes with lower isopropanol intermediates would not infringe claims 10(i) and 11.
GSK said the proposed processes were hypothetical, might not work, and could not be prepared for trial by the fixed date.
Laddie J refused to order the declaration trial to be heard with the other proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application in the Patents Court for an order that a section 71 declaration action be tried with related revocation and infringement proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; expedited main trial proceeded without the declaration action.
enrichment.ratio: Even where section 71 declarations may raise overlapping construction issues, a court should refuse conjoined trial where the opposing party cannot fairly be ready by the expedited date, Apotex made the application late without explaining delay, and Pumfrey J could in any event delineate claim scope in the main judgment without a separate declaration proceeding.
legal_issues: Whether hypothetical section 71 declarations should be entertained
Discretion to hear declaration proceedings with revocation and infringement actions
Fairness of expedited timetable to GSK
Whether urgency justified the late application

linked_authorities.name: Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing Co v Plastus Kreato AB

confidence.notes: Short procedural judgment; commercial context and refusal reasons are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Fair rent cap upheld despite section 70 errors
key_facts: Howard De Walden Estates appealed rent assessment committee determinations for three regulated flats at Crofton House, Marylebone.
The landlord spent about £135,000 on common-part improvements and sought uncapped fair rents above the Maximum Fair Rent Order cap.
The committee capped rents at roughly £8,250–£8,434 despite uncapped figures of about £13,500–£15,561.
The committee rejected the landlord's index-based method for showing improvements caused a more than 15% increase.
Elias J found errors on scarcity area and 30% deduction reasoning but dismissed the appeal because Article 2(7) cap application was lawful.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated appeal to the High Court against London Rent Assessment Committee fair rent redeterminations after Silber J quashed an earlier decision for inadequate reasons on Article 2(7).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; capped rents stood; appellant ordered to pay 50% of the committee's costs.
enrichment.ratio: On Article 2(7) the committee lawfully compared what the uncapped fair rent would have been without the improvements rather than attributing rent increases to market indices; where the Order applies the capped rent is decisive and errors in uncapped section 70 calculations need not be remitted unless repeal of the Order is likely.
legal_issues: Application of Article 2(7) where improvements allegedly increased rent by more than 15%
Section 70 market rent methodology and scarcity deduction
Adequacy of committee reasons on scarcity area and quantum
Whether security of tenure should increase market rent under section 70(1)
index_terms: Curtis v London Rent Assessment Committee

enrichment.short_title: Sri Lankan Tamil return risk and forehead scarring
key_facts: A 22-year-old Sri Lankan Tamil claimed asylum after low-level LTTE assistance, nine days' detention in May 1999 and visible forehead scarring.
The adjudicator accepted ill-treatment and scarring but found no real risk on return, noting he left Sri Lanka easily with the scar visible.
The IAT upheld the decision, treating scarring in individual context and doubting the forehead scar was torture-related for airport risk purposes.
UNHCR and Home Office country material said scarred returnees may face rigorous questioning depending on individual circumstances.
Simon Brown LJ held the IAT's fact-specific assessment was sustainable despite imperfect drafting in paragraph 13.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal dismissal of an asylum appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: Risk on return from scarring is assessed on the individual facts of each case, not by mechanically applying UNHCR categories; where authorities would learn of brief past detention, army medical treatment and release, a prominent but explainable forehead scar does not necessarily establish a real risk of further persecution or intensive interrogation on return.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT erred in approach to scarring and risk on return
Consistency between accepting torture-related scarring and finding no 'obviously combat or torture-related' scarring
Application of UNHCR guidance on obvious scarring
Relevance of ease of exit with facial scarring

confidence.notes: Short appeal on a familiar scarring point; tribunal findings treated as expert fact-specific assessment.

enrichment.short_title: Planning section 73 variation of HGV parking condition
key_facts: 1985 permission allowed two HGVs on woodland at Farthing Hill Wood to be parked only by occupiers of adjacent Farthing Hill House.
Gareth Rees's son sought to vary condition 2 so benefit enured to the woodland owner after the house was sold in 1998.
Monmouthshire refused; an inspector allowed the appeal under section 73, treating it as deleting and substituting the condition.
The council argued wider planning policies and enforcement disputes should be considered beyond the condition alone.
Mackay J held section 73 limited the inquiry to conditions where the original permission remained capable of implementation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to quash an inspector's decision allowing a section 78 appeal against refusal to vary a planning condition.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; inspector's decision upheld; defendant's costs summarily assessed at £4,592.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 73 the authority or inspector considers only the conditions subject to which planning permission should be granted; where the 1985 permission for two lorries on defined land remains implementable, varying a personal-user condition to tie benefit to woodland ownership does not require reopening the original grant's planning merits, following Powergen and Pye.
legal_issues: Scope of section 73 — conditions only versus wider planning considerations
Whether original permission remained capable of implementation
Relevance of enforcement history and alleged breaches of condition 1
Whether Condition 2 was imposed for planning or merely definitional reasons

linked_authorities.name: R v Leicester City Council ex p Powergen UK Ltd
Pye v Secretary of State for the Environment

confidence.notes: Inspector's section 73 analysis and Powergen application are clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Workplace stress claim fails Hatton foreseeability threshold
key_facts: Mrs Bonser sued RJB Mining for psychiatric injury from workplace stress between 1995 and 1998.
She held three competing responsibilities under a demanding manager, Mr Altounyan, and worked long hours.
In August 1996 she cried to a colleague about holiday work pressure but had no prior stress breakdowns at this employer.
The judge found breach in summer 1996 and awarded damages for accelerating breakdown by one year; medical evidence said intervention after December 1996 would have achieved little.
The Court of Appeal held employers must foresee injury to health, not merely stress from overwork, and August 1996 tears did not meet Hatton's plain-indications threshold.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against a county court judgment awarding damages for psychiatric injury caused by occupational stress.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; judgment set aside with costs.
enrichment.ratio: Following Hatton v Sutherland, liability for stress-induced psychiatric injury requires foreseeability of harm to health; overwork causing stress and a single tearful complaint about holiday workload, without known vulnerability or clear signs of impending breakdown, do not impose a duty to take remedial steps because stress alone is not enough and employers are entitled to assume employees can withstand normal pressures unless indications of impending harm to health are plain.
legal_issues: Foreseeability of psychiatric injury versus foreseeability of stress
Whether August 1996 events triggered a duty to act under Hatton
Effect of pre-existing emotional vulnerability unknown to the employer
Whether breach could support only accelerated breakdown damages

confidence.notes: Direct application of Hatton; court unanimously reversed on foreseeability of health breakdown.

enrichment.short_title: Joint expert instruction restored after CPR 35.8 error
key_facts: Mr Yorke claimed about £2,800 for building work; Mr Katra disputed quality and acted partly in person.
A joint expert was ordered but Katra signed the joint instruction letter only after deleting two contractual background sentences.
District Judge Enzer struck out Katra's defence for non-compliance; later judges refused to set aside until Judge Hull dismissed Katra's appeal on form grounds.
Dyson LJ reconstituted as a High Court judge and transferred the case to the Court of Appeal; CPR 35.8 allows each party to give separate instructions to a joint expert.
The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal and ordered the expert letter sent in the form Katra had signed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal (transferred from High Court) against refusal to set aside striking out of defence for failure to comply with joint expert instruction order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; joint expert letter to be sent as signed by Katra; multiple costs orders adjusted.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR 35.8 each instructing party may give instructions to a single joint expert, so requiring signature of a unified letter containing the other side's contractual content was a mistaken basis for striking out; once that error is recognised, refusal to set aside the strike-out and dismissal of the appeal on procedural form alone cannot stand.
legal_issues: Construction of CPR 35.8 on joint expert instructions
Whether deletion of background sentences justified striking out
Whether Judge Hull could dismiss appeal for wrong form alone
Costs of prolonged interlocutory litigation in a small claim

confidence.notes: Procedural point clearly resolved on CPR 35.8; lengthy history but ratio is narrow.

enrichment.short_title: Terror libel survives strike-out; CFA chilling effect discussed
key_facts: Louis Szondy (Adam Moussa) sued the Sunday Telegraph over October and December 2001 articles linking him to al-Qaeda and Islamic extremism.
The defendant pleaded justification on reasonable grounds to suspect terror involvement and Reynolds qualified privilege.
The Telegraph applied to strike out or obtain summary judgment, arguing CFA-funded libel claims chill investigative journalism.
Eady J rejected abuse and summary judgment applications, struck parts of justification relying impermissibly on police suspicion, and permitted amendments.
Disputed facts on website work, Libya links and journalist conduct required trial; Chase v News Group principles governed 'reasonable grounds' pleading.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court hearing on strike-out, summary judgment and security-for-costs applications in a CFA-funded libel claim before trial.
enrichment.outcome: Defendant's strike-out and summary judgment applications dismissed; certain justification particulars struck out; claimant's amendments allowed.
enrichment.ratio: CFA funding of defamation claims may chill media defendants but Parliament extended CFAs to libel to widen access to justice, so courts should not treat sub-50% merits as automatic abuse; on summary judgment disputed primary facts and Reynolds responsible journalism issues cannot be pre-judged, and a plea of justification for 'reasonable grounds to suspect' must prove objective primary facts not mere police suspicion, following Lewis, Evans, Shah and Chase.
legal_issues: Whether CFA-funded libel claims are an abuse of process or require security
Summary judgment on justification and qualified privilege
Permissible pleading of 'reasonable grounds to suspect' terrorism
Repetition rule and conduct rule in justification
Article 10 chilling effect of CFAs and success fees

linked_authorities.name: Chase v News Group Newspapers Ltd

confidence.notes: Long interlocutory judgment; strike-out outcome and justification pleading rules are clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Residential-to-office use refused under housing policies
key_facts: Mr Fasuyi sought planning permission to change first-floor use at 24A Plumstead High Street from residential to office.
Greenwich refused, applying UDP policies H7 and S20 to prevent net loss of residential accommodation above shops.
The inspector dismissed the section 78 appeal on paper, treating the application as residential-to-office and not reopening planning history.
Fasuyi argued registers showed retail not residential use and that policy S19 might favour small offices in the shopping area.
Elias J dismissed the section 288 appeal; Saxby prevents treating a planning application as a determination that permission is not required.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 against an inspector's dismissal of a planning appeal on paper.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Secretary of State's costs summarily assessed at £1,766.75 after judicial reduction.
enrichment.ratio: An inspector may determine a section 78 appeal on the basis on which it was presented without adjudicating whether earlier use was authorised residential or retail; following Saxby, a planning application does not impliedly seek a ruling that planning permission is unnecessary, and policies H7 and S20 lawfully prevent loss of residential accommodation above shops.
legal_issues: Whether inspector should have considered alleged misdescription of existing residential use
Applicability of UDP policies H7, S19 and S20
Whether Saxby bars reopening use history on a change-of-use application
Adequacy of inspector's paper determination

linked_authorities.name: Saxby v Secretary of State for the Environment
Wells v Minister of Housing and Local Government
Western Fish Products Ltd v Penwith District Council

confidence.notes: Short planning challenge; Saxby and UDP policy application clearly reasoned.
